summary: Defines the Delegation Signer (DS) resource record, placed at a zone cut to show that the delegated zone is signed and that a given key is valid for it. It modified the original DNSSEC design for operational reasons. It has been replaced by RFCs 4033, 4034 and 4035.

eli5.summary: A parent folder tells you which stamp the child folder uses to prove its papers are real. That note is the DS record. Later documents, RFCs 4033 to 4035, replaced this one.

questions: how does dnssec link parent and child zones
what is the delegation signer record
how does ds link parent and child zones in dnssec
what is a null key in dnssec
subtitle: A record placed at the parent side of a DNS delegation that vouches for the child zone's signing key.

tldr.problem: The original DNSSEC design had the parent store and sign the child's whole KEY set, and required a NULL KEY record for every unsecure child. That meant heavy two-way communication and wasted space in large delegation zones.
tldr.mechanism: The Delegation Signer (DS) record sits only at the parent side of a zone cut and holds a key tag, algorithm, digest type and a digest of one of the child's keys. The child signs its own KEY set with that key, and the parent signs the DS record.
tldr.outcome: A delegation with a DS RRset is secure and one without is unsecure, so NULL KEYs are no longer needed. This RFC has been obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

today: RFC 3658 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, and was updated by RFC 3755 before that. Use those documents for the current DNSSEC specification.

sections.title: Why the Old Key Model Hurt
sections.content:
When the same data lives in two administratively different DNS zones, it tends to drift apart. The RFC cites measurements that 10-30% of delegations on the Internet have different NS RRsets at the parent and the child.

The DNSSEC design in RFC 2535 made the parent sign the child's KEY RRset, which needed frequent two-way communication. It also required the parent to store a NULL KEY record for every unsecure child, spending a whole signed RRset to say one bit: this child is not secure. For large delegation zones the RFC calls this a significant barrier to deployment.

Letting the KEY set hold keys for other protocols was also a problem: it could grow large, need frequent updates, and raise the chance of compromised keys.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school that had to write a long signed note for every kid who did not have a library card. That is a lot of paper just to say no, so this document finds a shorter way.

sections.title: The Delegation Signer Model
sections.content:
The new DS record (type code 43) resides only at the parent. It identifies the key or keys the child uses to self-sign its own KEY RRset. The chain of trust is now built from the parent KEY RRset, the DS RRset from the parent and the KEY RRset at the child, which the RFC says is cryptographically equivalent to using just KEY records.

The parent only needs to hear about changes to the keys that sign the child's apex KEY RRset. The child keeps full control of the rest, so it can roll its zone keys often without the parent knowing. There is no requirement to use separate Key Signing Key and Zone Signing Key roles, and small zones are expected to use one key.

Only secure delegations need extra data, a signed DS RRset, instead of a NULL KEY at every unsecure one. The main cost is that verifying a zone's KEY RRset takes two signature verifications instead of one.
sections.eli5: The parent only writes down which stamp the child uses on its main page. The child can change all its other stamps without telling anyone, but checking takes one extra look.

sections.title: The DS Record Format
sections.content:
The DS record carries four things: a key tag, an algorithm, a digest type and a digest of a child KEY record. The key tag is calculated as in RFC 2535. The digest is computed over the canonical name of the delegated domain followed by the whole RDATA of the KEY record (flags, protocol, algorithm and public key).

Digest type 0 is reserved and type 1 is SHA-1. For SHA-1 the DS RDATA is 24 bytes whatever the key size. The KEY record it points to must have protocol field 3 and flag bit 7 set to 1.

The text form is three numbers followed by the digest in hex, for example example. DS 12345 3 1 123456789abcdef67890123456789abcdef67890.

The algorithm and key tag help a resolver quickly find candidate keys. Hashing the name together with the key data ties the two firmly, and the short digest keeps delegation answers small.
sections.eli5: The DS record is like a fingerprint of the child's key plus a short label. It is small, but nobody can easily make a different key with the same fingerprint.

sections.title: How Servers and Resolvers Behave
sections.content:
Servers and resolvers that support DS must support the OK bit and larger message sizes. A delegation is only secure if it has a DS RRset; an NS RRset with no DS means the child is unsecure from the parent's point of view. A DS RRset must not appear at a non-delegation point or at a zone's apex, and each one must be signed by at least one of the parent zone's keys.

When a query has the OK bit, a referral must include the parent's copy of the child's NS RRset, followed by either the DS and its signature, or the NXT and its signature. If these do not fit, the TC bit must be set.

A server authoritative for the parent must answer a DS query from the parent's data, even if it also serves the child. A server that serves only the child answers as if the DS record does not exist, with NOERROR, the AA bit set and an empty answer section. The RFC gives five ordered rules for servers that are authoritative for a zone and its grandparent but not the parent, so that older caches do not wrongly label a server lame.

The resolver walks from a trusted key to the DS record to the child KEY. Parents must allow multiple DS records to support key roll-over and several algorithms.
sections.eli5: If you ask a school office about a student's badge, the answer comes from the main office, not from the classroom. The office must also hand out the list of badges together with the directions.

sections.title: A Flag Day, Not a Gradual Switch
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that DS is a major change: it is the first resource record that can appear only on the upper side of a delegation. It is not backwards compatible with RFC 2535 and needs a flag day for DNSSEC, with many old nameservers and resolvers needing an upgrade.

RFC 2535-compliant resolvers will assume DS-secured delegations are only locally secure. The DNSEXT Working Group decided that rapid adoption of DS was preferable to supporting both models, so the only option for early adopters is to upgrade as soon as possible. The RFC also changes related rules: KEY records are no longer added to the additional section, and the NULL KEY is obsoleted.
sections.eli5: It is like changing which side of the road everyone drives on. It does not work well if only some people switch, so everyone is asked to switch quickly.

sections.title: Security and Cost
sections.content:
The change is not believed to reduce overall security. The child still has to give its keys to the parent, and prudent parents will authenticate that exchange. The child just gains more local control of its own KEY RRset.

An attacker could in principle make a KEY that matches all the fields of a DS set, but the RFC calls this impractical. An attacker trying to match any DS record would need to generate on average at least 2^80 keys. Implementations that do not understand DS will treat zones secured this way as unsecure.

On cost, a simple A record lookup needs N delegations plus one RRset verified under RFC 2535, and 2N+1 with DS. The resolver also needs an extra query for the DS record, but the RFC says this is never worse than chasing NULL KEY records.
sections.eli5: Faking a matching fingerprint would take more tries than anyone could realistically do. The price is that checkers do a little extra work.
